lesson.title: Before You Balance: Predicting What a Reaction Will Do
lesson.summary: Reaction prediction combines reaction type patterns, the activity series, and the solubility rules to figure out what a reaction will produce before you ever balance an equation.
lesson.body:
Predicting a reaction means figuring out what products will form, if any, before you write a single formula. This is a skill built from three tools you already have. The reaction types overview gives you a small set of patterns, combination, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, and combustion, that cover the overwhelming majority of reactions you will see in a first year course. The activity series tells you whether a single replacement reaction will actually happen: a metal can only displace a less active metal (or hydrogen) from a compound, never a more active one. The solubility rules tell you whether a double replacement reaction produces a solid precipitate or just leaves you with a mixture of dissolved ions that do not react.

The general method is to first recognize which pattern the reactants fit, then apply the matching rule. If two aqueous ionic solutions are mixed, you are likely looking at a double replacement: the cations and anions swap partners, and you check the solubility rules to see if either new combination is insoluble. If a solid metal is dropped into a solution containing a metal ion, you are looking at a possible single replacement, and you check the activity series to see whether the free metal sits above the dissolved metal.

Take lead(II) nitrate solution mixed with potassium iodide solution, a classic double replacement. The cations, Pb2+ and K+, swap anions: NO3- and I-. That gives two candidate products, PbI2 and KNO3. The solubility rules mark most nitrates as soluble, so KNO3 stays dissolved, but they mark most iodides as insoluble when paired with lead, so PbI2 drops out as a solid. The molecular equation is:

Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq)

Notice the coefficient of 2 in front of KI: it is required both to balance nitrogen and potassium and because two iodide ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge on lead. The precipitate that forms, PbI2, is a bright yellow solid, one of the most visually distinctive precipitates in the lab.

Prediction becomes useful the moment you attach numbers to it. Suppose 25.0 mL of 0.100 M Pb(NO3)2 is mixed with an excess of KI solution. How much solid PbI2 forms? Moles of lead nitrate come first: 0.0250 L x 0.100 mol/L = 2.50 x 10^-3 mol. Because the equation shows a 1:1 ratio between Pb(NO3)2 and PbI2, moles of PbI2 formed also equal 2.50 x 10^-3 mol. The molar mass of PbI2 is 207.2 + 2(126.90) = 461.0 g/mol, so the mass of precipitate is 2.50 x 10^-3 mol x 461.0 g/mol = 1.15 g.

Notice that prediction and quantity are two separate steps done in order: first decide what forms using the reaction type, the activity series, or the solubility rules, and only then use the balanced equation to calculate how much. Skipping the first step and jumping straight to stoichiometry is one of the most common sources of error, because you cannot correctly balance or calculate for a product that was never going to form in the first place.
